question.explanationHtml:
Detailed Explanation:
In the sentence 'My friends who are studying in Italy will be at the party.', the phrase 'who are studying in Italy' is a relative clause that describes 'my friends'. However, in English, we can also use a reduced relative clause by omitting 'who are' and using the present participle (V-ing) form. So, 'My friends studying in Italy will be at the party.' is correct and natural. The other options are either grammatically incorrect or awkward.
  • A. My friends who studying in Italy will be at the party. (Clause): This option is incorrect because after 'who', we need a verb (are) before the present participle 'studying'. The correct form should be 'who are studying'.
  • B. My friends studying in Italy will be at the party. (Reduced relative clause): This is the correct answer. It uses a reduced relative clause, where 'who are' is omitted and 'studying' (present participle) directly modifies 'my friends'.
  • C. My studying in Italy friends will be at the party. (Phrase): This option is incorrect because the order of words is unnatural in English. We do not place the participle phrase before the noun in this way.
Related structure or vocabulary: Reduced relative clauses: When the relative pronoun (who/that) is the subject of the clause and the verb is in the continuous form, we can reduce 'who are studying' to 'studying'.

Related structure or vocabulary: Adjective order: Adjectives usually come before the noun they describe. Relative clauses: 'who was handsome' can be replaced by an adjective before the noun.
